author: reek
body: FAT over the payload's own block drivers (B3.2, FAT32 in H3b). The foreword `Fat16` chapter already knows FAT: its BPB parse, directory-entry decode, name matching, and path splitting are pure functions over a sector buffer, and this chapter reuses every one of them. What it cannot reuse is `Fat16`'s sector source: those functions call the `block-read-sector` builtin, which is a syscall. The Option A stub jumps straight to `opening` and configures no syscall path, so on this boot every read must go through `disk-read-sector` (AHCI, then legacy IDE).

author: reek
body: Reading a file writes bytes into a flat caller-supplied buffer. `Fat16`'s own reader accumulates a `List Integer` one byte at a time -- fine for a small config file, ruinous for a 2 MB seed, which is what B3.3 will ask for.

author: reek
body: The EFI System Partition's first LBA, found by walking the GPT: the header at LBA 1 names the partition-entry array, and the first entry whose type GUID is the ESP's carries the starting LBA. Returns 0 when the disk has no GPT or no ESP -- an honest zero, not a guess.

author: reek
body: Only the low 32 bits of each 64-bit GPT field are read: a boot medium with more than 2 TB of sectors before its ESP is not a stick.

author: reek
body: Four bytes of the type GUID are enough to name the ESP among the partition types a boot stick carries.

author: reek
body: A zero 16-bit FAT size is the structural mark of the 32-bit layout; the parse then maps FAT32's fields into the shared record as the chapter prose describes.

author: reek
body: The FAT32 root directory is an ordinary cluster chain named by the BPB, so its search IS the data-area search; only FAT16 has the fixed root region.

author: reek
body: A directory that lives in the data area is a cluster chain, so a miss in one cluster follows the FAT to the next.

author: reek
body: `e` is the entry matched at depth-1. A path continues only through a directory (attribute bit 4); a file in the middle of a path is a miss, not a silent success.

author: reek
body: Copy a file's bytes into `dest`, following the FAT chain. Returns the number of bytes written, which is the entry's size unless the chain ended early (a truncated or corrupt file -- report what was actually read, never what the directory claimed).

author: reek
body: Reading a 2 MB file one sector at a time costs two reads per sector: the data, and the FAT sector holding the next cluster. Instead load the FAT once, follow the chain in memory, and coalesce consecutive clusters into runs -- a freshly written file is contiguous, so a whole seed becomes a single bulk command (one DMA on AHCI). Fragmentation costs one command per run, never per sector.

author: reek
body: Length of the run of consecutive clusters starting at `cluster`, capped so a corrupt chain cannot spin: a run can never exceed the clusters the file still needs.

author: reek
body: Read a file into a caller-supplied buffer. The buffer must hold the file's size rounded up to a whole sector -- the last sector arrives whole, and trimming it is the caller's business.

author: reek
body: The 8.3 name is passed already space-padded to 11 characters, the way it sits in a directory entry ("IDENTITYDAT").

author: reek
body: The chain writer: the FAT is loaded once and the whole chain is built in memory, then flushed to both copies in bulk, then the data goes out in contiguous runs -- the write-side mirror of Bulk File Reading above. Every allocated cluster is marked end-of-chain the moment it is taken, so the free scan cannot hand the same cluster out twice, and the link to the next overwrites the mark as the chain grows; a volume that runs out mid-chain aborts before the flush, leaving the disk untouched.

author: reek
body: Writes are chunked at 64 sectors: a bulk transfer above 64 KB crosses the TRB boundary question rung 3 of the sitting ladder has never answered on metal, and a screenshot must not be the first thing to ask it.

author: val
body: The same mount also speaks FAT32 -- the format every vendor stick and every volume past two gigabytes actually carries. The volume record is shared: a FAT32 volume is recognized structurally (a zero 16-bit FAT size names the 32-bit layout, the same key Linux turns), its root-entry count is zero by construction (which is exactly how the rest of this chapter tells the two apart), vol-root-start holds the root directory's CLUSTER rather than a sector, and vol-fat-sectors comes from the 32-bit field. Three rules follow the width everywhere: FAT entries are four bytes whose top nibble is reserved (masked on read, PRESERVED on write); end-of-chain is a 28-bit compare, never the 16-bit sentinel -- on a large volume a perfectly valid cluster number exceeds 65528 and truncating it to the FAT16 test silently ends every long chain; and a directory entry's starting cluster carries a high word at offset 20 that the 16-bit decoder never reads.

author: val
body: The signature says the sector is a GPT header and nothing more. Both CRC32 fields the format carries were read by nobody until 2026-08-15, so a tampered or half-written table parsed exactly like a good one, and the ESP start LBA it hands out becomes the partition base every later read is relative to. A garbage LBA is caught downstream by the geometry guard, because the volume it lands on will not parse as FAT; an LBA moved to a DIFFERENT well-formed FAT is not, and that is the case the array CRC exists to stop.

author: val
body: The CRC is streamed a sector at a time and never held: the entry array is NumberOfPartitionEntries * SizeOfPartitionEntry, 16 KB at our own 128 x 128, and accumulating it into a buffer or a list would cost that much arena on a path with no GC. A read failure answers -1, which no CRC can be, so a short medium refuses rather than comparing against a fabricated zero.

author: val
body: UEFI computes the header CRC with the CRC field itself read as four zero bytes, over HeaderSize bytes and not over the whole sector.

author: val
body: NumberOfPartitionEntries and SizeOfPartitionEntry are the array CRC's OWN EXTENT, so they are geometry and must be checked BEFORE the CRC that depends on them: a corrupt count moves the window and a reader then computes a perfectly valid CRC over the wrong bytes. The array must also fit between its own LBA and FirstUsableLBA, which is where the table is required to live.

author: val
body: A partition entry's type GUID is all sixteen bytes; matching the first four accepts any type whose GUID happens to open with the ESP's first dword. The value is the foreword's `gpt-esp-type-guid` rather than a second copy here -- a GUID spelled twice is a GUID that can disagree with itself.

author: val
body: Cell 80 of the xHCI diagnostic block (map and growth ceiling in GopXhci). Zero is NOT ASKED, per that block's sentinel discipline.

author: val
body: Cell 83 is the WRITE stage, and it is a separate cell because 80 is the mount stage: a write that fails on a mounted volume leaves 80 reading 7 (ok) and names nothing. 83 is the next free index in that block and is under the 96-dword wipe ceiling, so it is cleared on metal rather than reading firmware residue.

author: val
body: Cell 88 is how many sectors the data run actually wrote. `gfat-w-data` says only that the run stopped short, and the metal reading of 2026-08-19 could not tell a medium that refuses the first sector of a long transfer from one that stops near the end.

author: val
body: 89 and 90 are the bank's truth, and they exist because a write's RETURN was believed over the file. The third grouped sitting (2026-08-19, `diag.img` C46DE4DD) came back with `DIAG.TXT` truncated at 4,577 bytes and the SUMMARY painting `bank=ok`: every append after the sink refusal was refused, the caller discarded the answer, and nothing downstream asked the medium what was actually there. 89 holds the size read back from the directory entry after the last write, and 90 holds the stage index plus one of the FIRST append that did not land, or zero while every one has.

author: val
body: The BPB fields are volume GEOMETRY: they decide WHERE every later read lands, not how much is read, so a bogus one is REFUSED, never clamped. Clamping a wrong geometry does not read less, it reads the wrong sectors and hands the caller confident garbage, and the desk reads the compiler's own source off this volume. The bounds are FAT invariants (external spec): sectors-per-cluster is a power of two through 128, at least one reserved sector, one or two FATs, a non-empty FAT, and fat-start / data-start landing inside the declared volume.

author: val
body: End-of-chain follows the volume's width: the 16-bit sentinel test on a FAT32 volume would silently end every chain at the first cluster number past 65528, which a large volume reaches in ordinary use. A failed FAT read answers end-of-chain in the right width, so a bad sector truncates a file instead of spinning the walk.

author: val
body: A cluster number arrives from a directory entry or a FAT slot, both of which are volume data we did not produce. `fat16-cluster-sector` turns it into an LBA by arithmetic alone, so a number above the volume's own limit addresses sectors past the medium. The sentinel test above cannot catch it: on FAT16 every value over 65528 already reads as end-of-chain, but on FAT32 the whole band from the cluster count to 268435447 is neither a sentinel nor addressable.

author: val
body: On FAT32 a directory entry's starting cluster has a high word at offset 20 that the 16-bit decoder never reads; a file placed past cluster 65535 on a big volume would otherwise resolve to the wrong low-word cluster and read someone else's bytes. The 32-bit scanner mirrors the foreword's walk exactly -- free entry ends the directory, long-name and label entries are skipped -- and fixes the decoded entry's cluster.

author: val
body: Disk bytes are ASCII; `code-to-char` wants a CCE code, so the byte goes through `from-unicode` first.

author: val
body: Write-stage codes for cell 83. The small-file path reports 1-7, the multi-cluster path 11-17, and 20 is a completed write. A code with 100 added is the same failure PLUS a failed rollback, which is the one outcome that leaves the volume dirty: the chain is allocated on disk with no directory entry behind it.

author: val
body: The FAT is allocated in whole sectors, so it always holds MORE entries than the volume has clusters. Per the spec data clusters number from 2 and the highest valid one is `vol-cluster-count + 1` (`fat16-last-cluster`); every entry above that is padding with no backing sectors behind it. The scan bound is therefore the volume's limit, and the FAT's own capacity only when a malformed BPB puts the capacity lower.

author: val
body: Scan the loaded FAT for the first free entry at cluster 2 or above. Free means the entry's CLUSTER bits are zero: FAT32's top nibble is reserved and may be dirty on a volume other tools have touched, so the read masks it off. Returns 0 when the volume is full.

author: val
body: Set one FAT entry in BOTH copies. Each copy is edited by reading the sector holding the entry, poking the bytes, and writing it back -- a FAT with two disagreeing copies is a corrupt volume. On FAT32 the entry's reserved top nibble is preserved, as the spec demands.

author: val
body: Write a directory entry into the located root slot: the 11-byte name, attribute 0x20 (archive), the starting cluster, and the size. The rest of the 32-byte entry is zeroed. The cluster's high word always lands at offset 20 -- zero on FAT16, load-bearing on FAT32.

author: val
body: The FAT reaches the disk LAST, after the data and the directory slot are both secured. A cluster marked used with nothing pointing at it is leaked storage no later mount can reclaim; a cluster holding data while the FAT still calls it free is invisible, and the next allocator overwrites it. Only the second is recoverable, so the order takes that risk and not the other one.

author: val
body: Measured 2026-08-19 on a 2,896,050-byte file, 5,657 sectors: the whole write is 57 s of a 59 s save, and the chunk size is not what decides it -- one call, 64-sector chunks and 8-sector chunks came out 56, 59 and 58 s. At about 306 VM exits a sector the transfer is one exit per 16-bit PIO word, so reporting per chunk costs nothing next to it.

author: val
body: The successor is read before the entry is cleared, or the walk loses the rest of the chain.

author: val
body: A cluster the FAT reports free can still be claimed by a live directory entry on a volume another tool has corrupted, and the allocator cannot see that from the FAT alone. This marks every cluster reachable from the root directory and refuses a new chain that lands in one.

author: val
body: The walk descends into subdirectories, because the file whose loss stops an ESP booting is `EFI/BOOT/BOOTX64.EFI` and it is two levels down: a root-only walk marks the `EFI` directory's own cluster and nothing inside it.

author: val
body: The caller's buffer must be readable to the size rounded up to a whole sector -- the tail of the last sector goes to the disk as it lies. gfat-load-fat allocates by raw heap bump, so a caller that wants the FAT buffer and the file buffer reclaimed brackets the whole write with __heap-save / __heap-restore.
